```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>Spreading a cost over the years</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

A sum paid now becomes a cost a year through the [capital recovery factor]{.lx-term term="capital-recovery-factor"}, CRF:

$$\text{CRF} = \frac{r}{1-(1+r)^{-n}}$$

- $r$ is the borrowing rate a year (here 7%, or the owner's) and $n$ the number of years (15). At 7% over 15 years, CRF ≈ 0.1098: $740,000 of equipment costs about $81,248 a year.
- [K3](k03-discounting.html) explains discounting; Analyst lesson [A1](a01-project-tea.html) builds a project's cash flows year by year.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>Letting a solver choose the sizes</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

- This lesson tests one size at a time. A sizing model chooses battery, generator and solar together, hour by hour, and can treat the hospital's survival as a rule rather than a cost.
- A rule ("survive 72 hours") and a cost ("an hour without power costs $9,000") can give different designs: the second weighs the rare long outages by how rarely they come.
- Modeler lesson [M5](m05-microgrid-size-and-run.html) sizes a microgrid that must survive an outage.

```{=html}
<p class="lx-lede">Three myths and one question, then a practice set of about 30 minutes.</p>
<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="a14-myth">
<!-- a14-myth:start (written from the model by the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="pays" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A microgrid that keeps a hospital open always pays for itself.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. Here a 2-hour battery comes out at −$48,849 a year on outages alone, and at +$5,151 with the campus's bill savings, if it is full at every outage.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="voll" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “The value of lost load is one number.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. In the 2025 co-op survey, per kWh not delivered in an 8-hour outage, a household would pay $3.22 to avoid it and a business lost $41.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="owner" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “If a microgrid saves money overall, its owner comes out ahead.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. The owner pays the capital and gains only through rates, a fee or the savings it keeps. Its borrowing rate moves the net too: +$3,682 a year at 10%, +$34,416 at 4%.</p></details>
</div>
<!-- a14-myth:end -->
</div>
<div class="lx-quiz" data-quiz="a14">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="expected" data-answer="b">
<p class="lx-qtext">Outages of 4 hours hit the campus 0.4 times a year, and the hospital loses $9,000 an hour. What do they cost the hospital in a year, on average?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">$3,600</li><li data-value="b">$14,400</li><li data-value="c">$36,000</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>$14,400: 0.4 outages × 4 hours × $9,000 an hour.</p></details>
</div>
</div>
<div id="a14-practice" class="lx-card">
<!-- a14-practice:start (written from the model by the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Practice · about 30 minutes on your own</p><p class="lx-hint">Use the numbers in the steps above (2025 dollars; the campus's are illustrative).</p><ol class="lx-fb-practice"><li><p><b>Expected outage hours.</b> Outages of 1, 4, 12, 36 and 72 hours happen 0.8, 0.4, 0.15, 0.06 and 0.02 times a year. How many hours without power a year, on average?</p><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>7.8 hours: 0.8 × 1 + 0.4 × 4 + 0.15 × 12 + 0.06 × 36 + 0.02 × 72.</p></details></li><li><p><b>The fifth hour of battery.</b> At $9,000 an hour, what does a battery's fifth hour save a year? Does it pay at $14,975?</p><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Outages longer than 4 hours happen 0.23 times a year, so it saves $2,070 a year: far below $14,975.</p></details></li><li><p><b>When the first hour passes.</b> At what cost of an hour without power would the battery's first hour save as much as it costs?</p><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>$14,975 ÷ 1.43 outages a year = $10,472 an hour. The fixed costs would still need covering.</p></details></li><li><p><b>Value against price.</b> To avoid a 24-hour outage, a household would pay $1.96 per kWh not delivered. How many times the 2025 U.S. residential average of 17.23¢ per kWh?</p><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>About 11 times.</p></details></li><li><p><b>The cost of borrowing.</b> The battery-and-generator design costs $740,000 to build, spread over 15 years. Its capital cost a year at 4% and at 10%?</p><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>$66,556 and $97,291: the same equipment, $30,734 a year apart.</p></details></li><li><p><b>The mill's hours.</b> Why does the mill at midday lower the village's cost per kWh, while the mill in the evening helps less?</p><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>At midday the panels run the mill directly: $0.31 falls to $0.23. In the evening the battery must grow from 40 to 70 kWh: $0.28.</p></details></li></ol>
<!-- a14-practice:end -->
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-card lx-real">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">In the real world</p>
<p>In the 2025 survey of rural co-op members, 65% of businesses said a three-day outage would shut them down, and 16% would keep going on backup generation (<a href="https://eta-publications.lbl.gov/sites/default/files/2026-10/ice_2.0_nreca_final_report_28oct2026.pdf">Berkeley Lab and partners, p. 11</a>).</p>
<p class="a14-bridge">Beyond outages, on-site energy can also change where a business chooses to build:</p>
<blockquote class="lx-excerpt" data-source="excerpt:supply-chain-mg"><p>Because the <span class="lx-term" data-term="transactive-energy">transactive energy</span> market brought a new revenue stream, locations with stronger renewables became competitive to establish facilities despite higher fixed and <span class="lx-term" data-term="logistics-cost">logistics cost</span>.</p><p>Contrary to intuition, energy storage systems, which balance intermittent power and uncertain load, had limited benefits for cost saving.</p><footer>From: Li et al. (2023), <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.apm.2023.02.014">Applied Mathematical Modelling</a>.</footer></blockquote>
<p class="lx-hint"><a href="../files/papers/li2023facility.html">Paper page and citation</a></p>
<ul class="lx-hint a14-holds"><li>Holds when: <span class="lx-term" data-term="stylized-network">stylized networks</span> with synthetic distances and costs, candidate sites in California, Arizona and Nevada, and one year, planned week by week for products and hour by hour for energy.</li><li>Leaves out: grid outages, which the studies do not model.</li></ul>
<p class="lx-hint">The full case: <a href="cf1-supply-chain-microgrids.html">case file CF1</a>.</p>
</div>
<div class="lx-card lx-sources">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Sources and further reading</p>

November 2026.</li>
<li>EIA. <a href="https://www.eia.gov/electricity/monthly/epm_table_grapher.php?t=epmt_5_3">Electric Power Monthly, Table 5.3: Average Price of Electricity to Ultimate Customers</a>. Released 23 October 2026.</li>
```
